payload_fields.seoTitle: BPC-157 Research Peptide | C62H98N16O22 | Amino Based
payload_fields.seoDescription: BPC-157 (GEPPPGKPADDAGLV): synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide. Chemical identity, preclinical research context, evidence limits. Research use only.
payload_fields.description: BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide (sequence GEPPPGKPADDAGLV) corresponding to a partial sequence of body protection compound, a protein identified in human gastric juice. It has also appeared in the literature under the development designations PL-14736, PLD-116 and PL-10. Amino Based supplies it as a lyophilised powder for laboratory research use only. The published evidence base is large but overwhelmingly preclinical, and no conclusion about human safety or efficacy can be drawn from it.
payload_fields.productDetailsTitle: BPC-157: Chemical Identity, Synonyms and Characterization
payload_fields.productDetailsDescription:
BPC-157 is a synthetic pentadecapeptide — a chain of fifteen amino acids — whose sequence, Gly-Glu-Pro-Pro-Pro-Gly-Lys-Pro-Ala-Asp-Asp-Ala-Gly-Leu-Val (single-letter code GEPPPGKPADDAGLV), corresponds to a partial sequence of a larger protein called body protection compound, or BPC, originally isolated from human gastric juice. The "157" identifies the specific fragment that has been studied; it does not refer to a dose, a concentration or a generation number. Because the peptide is produced by solid-phase synthesis rather than extracted from tissue, the material supplied for research is a defined synthetic molecule rather than a biological isolate.

Several names refer to the same molecule, which matters when searching the literature. In addition to BPC-157 and BPC 157, the compound appears in peer-reviewed papers as PL-14736, PLD-116 and PL-10 — development designations used by the Croatian pharmaceutical company Pliva — and is widely described by the phrase "stable gastric pentadecapeptide". In one registered clinical study it appears as the active ingredient of a formulation designated PCO-02. A literature search on "BPC-157" alone will therefore miss a meaningful part of the published record, particularly the clinical-development material from the early 2000s.

The free-base form has the molecular formula C62H98N16O22 and a molecular weight of approximately 1419.5 g/mol, indexed under CAS registry number 137525-51-0 and PubChem CID 9941957. This matters to anyone calculating molarity. Research-grade peptides of this class are very commonly supplied as an acetate salt rather than as the free base, and the acetate is a separate chemical entity with its own identifiers: CAS 216441-37-1, PubChem CID 155977614, formula written as C62H98N16O22 with acetic acid, molecular weight approximately 1479.59 g/mol. Using the free-base molecular weight for material that is in fact an acetate salt introduces a systematic error of roughly four per cent. Amino Based does not state which form applies to a given lot unless it is recorded on the lot-specific certificate of analysis; where no certificate has been published, the salt form is not independently verified from the available sources and should be confirmed before quantitative work.

For a linear peptide of this kind the amino acid sequence, read from the N-terminus, is the structural definition: it specifies the molecule completely, and a SMILES string or InChIKey adds no information that the sequence and the stated stereochemistry do not already carry. A canonical SMILES string and InChIKey for this compound were not independently verified from the sources available for this page, so none is reproduced here; researchers requiring a machine-readable structure should take it directly from the PubChem record for CID 9941957 rather than from a supplier listing.

Structurally, the sequence is notable for a proline-rich region near the N-terminus — three consecutive proline residues at positions three to five — and for containing no cysteine. The absence of cysteine means the peptide cannot form intramolecular disulfide bridges, so it has no fixed tertiary structure of the kind seen in cyclised peptides, and it is not subject to the oxidative disulfide scrambling that complicates the handling of cysteine-containing peptides. The proline content contributes conformational rigidity to that segment of the chain. The peptide carries three acidic residues (one glutamate, two aspartates) against a single basic residue (lysine), giving it a net negative charge at neutral pH.

The descriptor "stable gastric pentadecapeptide" reflects reports that the peptide resists degradation in human gastric juice over extended periods. That characterisation originates in the primary literature and describes behaviour observed under specific experimental conditions. It should not be read as a general claim about stability in any other medium, at any other temperature, or over any other timescale.

The material is supplied as a lyophilised white to off-white powder in a sealed glass vial, in nominal 5 mg and 10 mg presentations, where the stated quantity refers to the mass of material in the vial. Lyophilised peptides are hygroscopic, and the general laboratory convention is to let a sealed vial reach room temperature before opening it, so atmospheric moisture does not condense onto cold powder. Amino Based publishes no product-specific stability study for this peptide, so no shelf-life, reconstituted-stability or freeze-thaw tolerance figures are claimed. Where such data are needed for a protocol they should be established in the receiving laboratory or taken from a lot-specific certificate, not inferred from general statements about peptide handling.
payload_fields.researchFocusTitle: Research Focus, Clinical Record and Evidence Gaps
payload_fields.researchFocusDescription:
Published research on BPC-157 is extensive in volume but narrow in character, and understanding that shape matters more than counting papers. A review in Cell and Tissue Research examining the peptide's role in musculoskeletal soft tissue healing noted that studies had been performed overwhelmingly in small rodent models, that efficacy had not been confirmed in humans, and that across roughly two decades only a small number of research groups had carried out in-depth work on the compound (PMID 30915550, doi:10.1007/s00441-019-03016-8). That concentration of output within a limited set of laboratories is itself a methodological consideration, because independent replication across unrelated groups is one of the stronger indicators that a finding will generalise.

The human clinical record deserves to be stated precisely, because it is frequently misrepresented in both directions. BPC-157 did enter clinical development. Primary research papers from 2003 and 2005 describe it as then being in clinical trials for inflammatory bowel disease under the designations PL-14736, PLD-116 and PL-10 (Pliva), with one describing it as at "clinical phase II" (PMID 14554208, doi:10.1016/S0736-0266(03)00110-4; PMID 15840402, doi:10.1016/j.ejphar.2005.02.033). Separately, a Phase I pilot study in healthy volunteers is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT02637284: a randomised, placebo-controlled study of orally administered PCO-02 tablets containing 1 mg of BPC-157, with a planned enrolment of 42 subjects, sponsored by PharmaCotherapia and conducted at Hospital Ángeles Tijuana, with a registry completion date of March 2016. That registration lists no posted results and its recruitment status is recorded as unknown.

So the accurate summary is neither "there are no human studies" nor "it has been clinically validated". Human clinical work was initiated more than twenty years ago, but no completed controlled efficacy results for BPC-157 appear in the peer-reviewed literature, and a 2026 review of the compound's biopharmaceutical and translational development barriers notes the absence of a completed Phase II trial (PMID 42198317). Clinical development that starts and then produces no published outcome is a weaker signal than no development at all would be neutral, because unpublished trial data cannot be assessed.

The largest body of experimental work concerns tissue repair. Studies in rodent models have examined BPC-157 in tendon, ligament and skeletal muscle injury — an early and frequently cited example reported accelerated healing of transected rat Achilles tendon alongside in vitro effects on cultured tendocytes (PMID 14554208) — and a review in Frontiers in Pharmacology surveyed wound-healing models more broadly (PMID 34267654, doi:10.3389/fphar.2021.627533). Related reviews address intestinal anastomosis models in rats (PMID 39204186, doi:10.3390/ph17081081), experimental fistula models (PMID 32329684), striated, smooth and cardiac muscle (PMID 36551977, doi:10.3390/biomedicines10123221), and ocular models including experimental glaucoma (PMID 37513963, doi:10.3390/ph16071052). A 2025 literature and patent review in Pharmaceuticals catalogued the breadth of reported activity and the surrounding patent landscape (PMID 40005999, doi:10.3390/ph18020185).

Two mechanistic themes recur. The first is an interaction with nitric oxide signalling: a review in Current Pharmaceutical Design is devoted specifically to the reported BPC-157 and NO-system relationship (PMID 23755725), and experiments in this line typically use NO-synthase inhibitors and NO donors to probe whether an observed effect depends on that pathway. The second is angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, with studies examining vascular endothelial growth factor receptor signalling in injured tissue. Separate work has investigated effects in the central nervous system (PMID 34380875, doi:10.4103/1673-5374.320969) and along the brain-gut axis (PMID 27138887, doi:10.2174/1570159x13666160502153022).

These themes should be read carefully. A reported association between a peptide and a signalling pathway in an animal model establishes that the pathway was implicated under those conditions. It does not establish a receptor, a binding affinity, or a defined mechanism of action. No specific high-affinity receptor for BPC-157 has been established in the published literature, so the mechanism is better described as proposed and incompletely characterised than as known — a meaningful distinction for experimental design, because a compound without an identified receptor cannot be positioned within a pathway by inference alone.

The remaining evidence gaps are substantial. The overwhelming majority of published work is in rats and mice, and findings from rodent injury models cannot be extrapolated to humans. Where pharmacokinetic work exists it has been conducted in animals: a study characterising pharmacokinetics, distribution, metabolism and excretion was performed in rats and dogs. Reporting of negative or null results appears limited, raising the ordinary concern about publication bias. Dose-response characterisation is inconsistent between studies and routes of administration vary widely, which complicates direct comparison.

For researchers designing experiments, the practical implication is that BPC-157 should be treated as an incompletely characterised investigational compound rather than a well-defined tool molecule. Positive and vehicle controls, independent confirmation of peptide identity and purity, and endpoints fixed before data collection all carry more weight than usual where the literature is concentrated in few groups and skewed toward positive findings. Further research — particularly independent replication and properly controlled, published human investigation — is required before any conclusion about clinical relevance would be warranted.
payload_fields.qualityPurityTitle: Analytical Verification and What Is Actually Documented
payload_fields.qualityPurityDescription:
Amino Based publishes analytical results on a per-lot basis. Where a lot-specific certificate of analysis has been issued for this product it is available from the Certificates page, and any purity figure displayed on this page is taken directly from that certificate and stated exactly as recorded. Where no certificate has been published for a lot, no analytical result is claimed for it here, and the absence of a figure should be read as the absence of a published measurement rather than as an implied standard.

Researchers evaluating any supplier's peptide material look for two distinct categories of evidence, and it is worth separating them because they answer different questions. Identity confirmation, typically by mass spectrometry, answers whether the molecule in the vial is the intended sequence, by comparing the observed mass against the mass calculated for that sequence. Purity assessment, typically by reverse-phase high-performance liquid chromatography, answers what proportion of the material is the target peptide rather than truncated sequences, deletion sequences, or residual synthesis reagents. A document reporting only one answers only half the question. When reading an HPLC purity figure, the detection wavelength, the gradient and the integration method all affect the number, which is why a percentage quoted without its chromatogram is weaker evidence than one accompanied by the trace.

Two further points are specific to peptides of this class. First, lyophilised peptide mass is not the same as peptide content: a vial labelled 10 mg may contain counter-ions and residual water alongside the peptide, and where peptide content has not been separately determined by amino acid analysis or a comparable method, the stated mass is a fill mass rather than a verified peptide mass. Second, as set out in the characterisation section above, the salt form materially affects molar calculations and should be confirmed rather than assumed.

Amino Based has not performed independent laboratory testing, manufacturing validation, or primary research on this compound beyond what is recorded on any published lot certificate, and makes no claim of third-party accreditation, pharmaceutical-grade manufacture, or regulatory approval for this product.
payload_fields.complianceNoticeTitle: Research Use Only: Regulatory Status and Researcher Responsibilities
payload_fields.complianceNoticeDescription:
This product is supplied for laboratory research use only (RUO). It is not for human or veterinary use. It is not a drug, a dietary supplement, a cosmetic, a food or a medical device, and it has not been evaluated or approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration, or by any other regulatory authority, for any therapeutic indication. It must not be used in the diagnosis, treatment, cure, mitigation or prevention of any disease or condition, in humans or in animals. Sale is restricted to qualified researchers, laboratories and scientific institutions. Nothing on this page constitutes medical advice, and no administration, dosing or reconstitution guidance for human or veterinary use is provided here or available on request.

Two regulatory facts are worth stating, because they are frequently misunderstood and because they bear directly on the legitimate research context for this compound. BPC-157 has been included on the World Anti-Doping Agency Prohibited List, which means its use is prohibited for athletes subject to anti-doping rules. Separately, BPC-157 has been considered by the United States Food and Drug Administration in the context of pharmacy compounding, including review by the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee; it is not an approved active pharmaceutical ingredient. Neither point constitutes a safety determination in either direction. Together they establish that this is not an approved therapeutic agent and that it is subject to regulatory restriction in defined contexts.

The existence of historical clinical-trial activity does not change that status. A compound that entered Phase I or Phase II investigation and did not complete development to approval is, in regulatory terms, an unapproved investigational substance — not a partially approved one. Registration of a trial is not evidence of efficacy, and an unpublished trial result is not evidence of anything at all.

It should also be stated clearly that labelling a substance "research use only" describes the supplier's intended use and the terms on which the material is sold. It is not, in itself, a determination of legal status, and it does not exempt a purchaser from applicable law. Researchers remain responsible for compliance with the law in their own jurisdiction, for institutional review and biosafety approvals where their work requires them, for any import and export controls applying to shipments of research chemicals, and for safe handling and disposal of the material.

Standard institutional practice for handling lyophilised peptide powders applies: appropriate personal protective equipment, handling in a suitable containment environment to avoid aerosolising fine powder, and disposal of vials and residual solutions in accordance with institutional chemical and biohazard waste protocols. Finally, the preclinical character of the literature described above bears repeating in a compliance context. Findings from rodent injury models do not demonstrate safety in humans, do not demonstrate efficacy in humans, and must not be presented or interpreted as evidence of either.

faqs.question: What exactly is BPC-157?
faqs.answer: BPC-157 is a synthetic peptide of fifteen amino acids, sequence GEPPPGKPADDAGLV. That sequence corresponds to a fragment of a larger protein called body protection compound (BPC), originally identified in human gastric juice. The material supplied for research is produced by chemical synthesis rather than extracted from tissue, so it is a defined synthetic molecule. The number 157 identifies the particular fragment studied; it is not a dose, a concentration or a version number.

faqs.question: What other names does BPC-157 go by?
faqs.answer: The same molecule appears in the literature as BPC 157, PL-14736, PLD-116 and PL-10 — the latter three being development designations used by the Croatian company Pliva — and is widely described by the phrase "stable gastric pentadecapeptide". In one registered clinical study it is the active ingredient of a formulation called PCO-02. This matters practically: searching only for "BPC-157" will miss much of the clinical-development literature from the early 2000s, which is indexed under the Pliva designations.

faqs.question: What is its molecular formula and molecular weight, and why do sources disagree?
faqs.answer: The free base has the molecular formula C62H98N16O22 and a molecular weight of approximately 1419.5 g/mol (CAS 137525-51-0, PubChem CID 9941957). Sources appear to disagree because peptides of this class are frequently supplied as an acetate salt, which is a different chemical entity: C62H98N16O22 with acetic acid, molecular weight approximately 1479.59 g/mol, CAS 216441-37-1. Both figures are correct for their respective forms. Calculating molarity with the free-base weight for material that is actually the acetate salt puts your concentrations out by roughly four per cent.

faqs.question: Have there been human clinical trials of BPC-157?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the record is incomplete, and this is the single most misrepresented point about the compound. Papers from 2003 and 2005 describe BPC-157 as then in clinical trials for inflammatory bowel disease under the designations PL-14736, PLD-116 and PL-10, one of them placing it at clinical phase II. A Phase I pilot study in 42 healthy volunteers using an oral formulation is registered as NCT02637284, with a registry completion date of March 2016. That registration lists no posted results and its status is recorded as unknown. No completed controlled efficacy results for BPC-157 appear in the peer-reviewed literature. So the compound did enter clinical development, and that development did not produce published outcomes.

faqs.question: Does BPC-157 have a known receptor or an established mechanism of action?
faqs.answer: No specific high-affinity receptor for BPC-157 has been established in the published literature. Experimental work has repeatedly implicated nitric oxide signalling and angiogenic pathways, including vascular endothelial growth factor receptor signalling, in effects observed in animal models. Implicating a pathway is not the same as establishing a mechanism: it shows the pathway was involved under those particular experimental conditions. The mechanism is best described as proposed and incompletely characterised rather than known.

faqs.question: How does BPC-157 differ from the BPC protein it is derived from?
faqs.answer: Body protection compound is a protein found in gastric juice. BPC-157 is a short synthetic fragment corresponding to part of that protein, not the protein itself. The two are not interchangeable, and findings reported for one should not be attributed to the other. The distinction matters when reading older literature, where terminology is not always consistent, and when comparing supplier documentation that may describe the material imprecisely.

faqs.question: What does the published research actually investigate?
faqs.answer: Most of it examines tissue repair in rodent injury models: tendon, ligament and skeletal muscle injury, wound healing, intestinal anastomosis and fistula models. An early and frequently cited study reported accelerated healing of transected rat Achilles tendon together with in vitro effects on cultured tendocytes. Smaller bodies of work address striated, smooth and cardiac muscle, ocular models including experimental glaucoma, the central nervous system, and the brain-gut axis. Review articles covering each area are indexed in PubMed and are the most efficient entry point into the primary literature.

faqs.question: What are the main limitations of the current evidence?
faqs.answer: Four stand out. Almost all published work is in rats and mice, and rodent injury-model findings cannot be extrapolated to humans. Human clinical development was initiated but produced no published controlled efficacy results. The literature is concentrated in a small number of research groups, which limits independent replication — a point made explicitly in a 2019 review in Cell and Tissue Research. And the record is weighted toward positive findings with little reporting of null results, raising the ordinary concern about publication bias. Dose-response characterisation and routes of administration also vary widely between studies, which makes cross-study comparison difficult.

faqs.question: What does "research use only" mean, and is this product legal to buy?
faqs.answer: Research use only describes the terms on which the material is sold and the supplier intended use: laboratory research, not human or veterinary consumption. It is not a legal classification, and it does not exempt a purchaser from applicable law. Legality depends on your jurisdiction and on what you do with the material. Researchers are responsible for their own regulatory compliance, including institutional approvals, import and export controls, and safe disposal. Amino Based cannot advise on the legal position in any particular jurisdiction.

faqs.question: What should I verify before relying on a supplier purity figure?
faqs.answer: Ask for two separate things, because they answer different questions. Mass spectrometry confirms identity — that the molecule present is the intended sequence. Reverse-phase HPLC assesses purity — what proportion of the material is the target peptide rather than truncated or deletion sequences and residual reagents. A certificate reporting only one answers half the question. For an HPLC figure the chromatogram matters as much as the percentage, because detection wavelength, gradient and integration method all affect the number. Note also that a labelled vial mass is a fill mass unless peptide content has been determined specifically, and confirm the salt form before any molar calculation.
